title: Homepage hero — engineering assurance variants
content:
Goal
---
Fast iteration doc for hero and above-the-fold copy variants aimed at engineering and platform buyers. We want a set of 6–8 concise hero directions that emphasize the production-first thesis (latency, cost, reliability) but also speak to platform teams who need predictable capacity, private deployments, and control. This is deliberately more technical and assurance-oriented than the pure growth headlines.

Primary audiences
- Software engineers building LLM features (dev-first language)
- Platform/infra leads and SREs evaluating operational guarantees
- Product managers at mid-market/enterprise assessing TCO and risk

Success metrics (experiment / launch)
- 1. CTR on primary CTA (Start for free / Try API) — target +10% vs baseline hero
- 2. Time to first API call from sign-up funnel — reduce by 15% (signal of technical clarity)
- 3. Demo request rate from Enterprise contact form — +8% (signal of enterprise resonance)

Positioning pillars to surface in hero and subhead
1) Production-grade performance: measurable latency and throughput.
2) Cost transparency + levers: batching, caching, quantization controls.
3) Deployment flexibility: hosted API -> dedicated -> private (same API surface).
4) Reliability & graceful degradation: fallback model variants, regional routing.
5) Developer ergonomics: quick onboarding, SDKs, and reproducible rollouts.

Tone guidance- Direct, engineering-friendly; avoid marketing fluff. Use concrete verbs (serve, route, pin, cache). When claiming performance, pair with a metric or mechanism. Avoid opaque buzzwords like "AI-native" without context.

Hero variants (short, single-line taglines) — aim for 6 seed options
1) "Predictable LLM inference — latency, cost, and reliability you can measure"
2) "Ship LLM features that stay fast and cheap at scale"
3) "One API for hosted, reserved, and private inference — same behavior everywhere"
4) "Inference you can trust: SLOs, fallbacks, and customer-grade capacity"
5) "Control the economics of every token — batching, cache, and quantize options"
6) "Run giant models in production without guessing your unit costs"

Subhead / above-the-fold explainer lines (pairs to test under each hero)
A) "Unified runtime, transparent economics, and rollout tools for production LLMs. Start with our hosted API and scale to dedicated or private deployments on your timeline."
B) "High-throughput GPU runtime plus smart routing and caching so your app stays fast and predictable as usage grows."
C) "Pin model versions, run canary rollouts, and fallback automatically when capacity dips — built for product reliability."
D) "Per-token cost breakdowns, autoscaling options, and quantization recommendations that save real dollars on inference."

Primary CTAs to test
- Primary: "Start free / Get an API key"
- Secondary: "Compare performance profiles" (links to perf catalog)
- Enterprise CTA: "Talk to sales — SLA & private options"

Microcopy and scaffolding ideas (small experiments)
- A tiny line under CTA: "No credit card required — 10k tokens free" (A/B with none)
- Micro-badge strip: icons + short labels: "Hosted API" | "Dedicated capacity" | "Private deployment"
- Quick stat row possibilities: "< 50ms median token latency • 20% token cost saved with Optimize" (only use if we have verified numbers)

Competitive differentiator notes (short competitive analysis bullets)
- Compared to hyperscaler managed endpoints: Emphasize turnkey, model-agnostic cost controls and optimized kernels. Hyperscalers sell infra, we sell inference runtime & developer UX baked for LLM patterns.
- Compared to API-first LLM providers: We compete on economics and deterministic serving for production apps, rather than pure model access. Messaging should avoid implying better model quality — focus on production outcomes.
- Compared to self-hosted runtimes: Highlight unified cloud-native option + private deployment path. Sell the "same API, different ops model" story: customers can start hosted and migrate to private/dedicated without rewriting app logic.

Dos and don'ts (copy guardrails)
- Do: Call out specific levers (batching, KV cache, quant profiles) that engineers recognize.
- Do: Use measurable language (latency, throughput, cost per 1k tokens) when claims are backed by a linked perf doc.
- Don’t: Use vague phrases like "faster AI" or "best models" without a clear qualifier.
- Don’t: Overpromise absolute uptime SLOs on the public homepage — save contractual claims for enterprise pages.

Hero variants with short supporting bullets (one-liners under hero) — full set for experimentation
Variant A (assurance):
Hero: "Predictable LLM inference — latency, cost, and reliability you can measure"
Support: "Per-route dashboards, token-level cost breakdowns, and canary rollouts so you never guess production behavior."
CTA: "Try the hosted API"

Variant B (practical velocity):
Hero: "Ship LLM features that stay fast and cheap at scale"
Support: "SDKs, quickstart templates, and smart batching that cut token spend without sacrificing latency."
CTA: "Get an API key"

Variant C (ops-first):
Hero: "One API for hosted, reserved, and private inference — same behavior everywhere"
Support: "Move from hosted to dedicated or private without changing client code; preserve rollouts and performance profiles."
CTA: "See deployment modes"

Variant D (cost-control):
Hero: "Control the economics of every token — batching, cache, and quantize options"
Support: "Automated suggestions from Redwood Optimize plus deployable quantized model variants for production savings."
CTA: "Optimize my workload"

Variant E (reliability):
Hero: "Inference you can trust: SLOs, fallbacks, and customer-grade capacity"
Support: "Built-in fallback chains and regional routing keep apps online when hot-serving capacity drops."
CTA: "Request enterprise info"

Quick UX/engineering notes for design handoff- Keep hero copy tight (max 8–10 words ideally).
- Subhead should be 1–2 sentences introducing the 3 pillars (performance, economics, deployments).
- Include small lockup of icons showing deployment modes to reduce cognitive load.
- For developer-centric flows, show a one-line example curl request near CTA (familiar language pattern helps reduce friction).

Measurement plan for experiments
- Launch A/B with 3 hero variants: Assurance (A), Practical (B), Ops-first (C). 50/50 traffic split to control and combine with a personal-test cohort of developer signups from existing ads.
- Track funnel events: hero CTA click, signup, first API request, time to first token.
- Run for 10k unique visitors minimum or 2 weeks, whichever is longer.

Open questions / risks
- Do we have audited numbers (latency medians, cost savings) to put in a stat row? If not, risk of making claims. Action: link to perf-catalog doc (CONFLUENCE-ENG-HERO-2026).
- How much product jargon is too much for PMs vs engineers? We'll A/B test a small copy variant with less tooling language.
- Legal review required for any quantifiable claims about cost/latency. Add legal to reviewer list before pushing any numeric badges.

Next steps (immediate)
1) Pick three hero directions for variant A/B test by 2026-02-05. Owner: Maya.
2) Designer: create 3 quick comps showing hero + curl snippet + small stat row. Owner: Evan. Due: 2026-02-12.
3) Engineering: ensure the quickstart curl and SDK snippet are up-to-date in the docs. Owner: Ravi. Due: 2026-02-09.
4) Legal/Comms: review microcopy that includes numbers. Owner: Sofia. Due: 2026-02-18.

Notes / freeform brainstorm (raw)
- Could we do a micro-interactive hero: user picks their constraint (latency/cost/privacy) and the page adapts to show recommended deployment? Nice UX but higher implementation cost.
- Consider a short tagline for marketing channels: "Inference that scales — not just technically, financially." Might be useful for retargeting ads.
- Customer quote slot: engineering-focused testimonial: "Switched to Redwood and cut 30% off token cost while staying within 75ms p95 latency" — only use if we have a verified case study.

Attachments & references
- Perf catalog: CONFLUENCE-ENG-HERO-2026 (linked)
- Homepage repo PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/marketing/PR-58
- UX tickets: JIRA-UX-1428

End of doc
